Article Title: New York's Plaza Hotel opened in 1907 and last shut for a $450 million overhaul; 119 years later, the 282-room landmark will close again for at least four years to restore its historic facade
Article Text:
Photo credit: The Plaza website

A landmark on fifth Avenue

Why the facade needs work

A four-year closure

Photo credit: The Plaza/ Instagram

Previous closures and renovations

A cultural symbol of New York

What the closure means

New York City’s Plaza Hotel is preparing to close again, this time for a restoration of its landmark-protected facade. The hotel, which opened in 1907, will shut from January 2027 for at least four years while crews carry out repair and preservation work on the 119-year-old building. The Plaza said the project reflects the complexity of maintaining a property of such architectural and historical significance, with careful attention to preservation requirements, long-term care, and public safety.The closure will be one of the longest in the hotel’s modern history. It follows the Plaza’s 2005 to 2008 shutdown for a $450 million lobby-to-roof restoration, and its more than year-long pandemic closure in 2020. This time, however, the work is focused on the exterior rather than a full interior transformation.The Plaza Hotel opened in 1907 at Fifth Avenue and 59th Street, overlooking Central Park. For more than a century, it has been recognised for its architectural character, exceptional craftsmanship, and enduring presence in Manhattan. The building is landmark-protected, meaning any restoration must follow historic preservation requirements.The Plaza said the facade work requires detailed planning and coordination with relevant stakeholders, which is one reason the closure is expected to last at least four years.The hotel has 282 rooms and remains one of New York’s most recognisable addresses. Its location beside Central Park has made it a recurring backdrop for films, television, literature, and high-profile social events.The New York City Department of Buildings told CBS News that its most recent inspection found the Plaza’s facade unsafe. That finding is why a sidewalk shed has been required around the building. The department also said there was nothing on the city’s end preventing the hotel from remaining open while repairs were carried out. The decision to close entirely appears to be driven by the scale and intrusion of the restoration work rather than a city order to shut down.Facade inspections are an important safety measure in New York, where older buildings can shed masonry, metal, or other materials if deterioration is not addressed. For a landmark as prominent as the Plaza, repairs must also meet preservation standards that protect its historic appearance.The Plaza will close in January 2027 and remain shut for at least four years. The hotel said the significant intrusion into operations made a full closure necessary while the facade work proceeds. The announcement did not include a cost estimate or a detailed list of planned repairs. Officials said further considerations relating to planning and execution remain under review as the process advances.The long timeline reflects the difficulty of restoring a protected historic building in one of the world’s busiest urban environments. Workers will need to balance safety, preservation, construction logistics, and the expectations of residents, guests, and neighbours.The Plaza has closed before, but rarely for this long. From 2005 to 2008, it underwent a $450 million restoration that covered the building from lobby to roof, as per reports.That project transformed parts of the hotel into private residences while preserving its historic public spaces. It was one of the most ambitious hotel conversions in New York, and it helped reposition the Plaza as both a luxury hotel and a residential landmark.The hotel also closed for more than a year during the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. That shutdown was driven by public health restrictions and the collapse in travel demand, rather than construction work.The Plaza is more than a hotel. It has appeared in films including 'Home Alone 2', 'Bride Wars', and 'The Great Gatsby', and it is central to Kay Thompson’s classic children’s books 'Eloise at the Plaza' and 'Eloise at Christmastime'.Its name has become shorthand for old-world luxury in New York. The hotel’s ballrooms, afternoon tea service, and Central Park-facing suites have made it a destination for visitors, celebrities, and New Yorkers alike. That cultural importance is part of why the facade restoration matters. The Plaza is not simply maintaining a building; it is preserving a piece of the city’s architectural and social history.The four-year closure will affect guests, employees, and the full-time residents who live in the hotel. CBS News reported that it is unclear how those residents will be affected by the restoration.For travellers, the closure means one of New York’s most iconic hotels will be unavailable for an extended period. For preservationists, it represents a necessary investment in keeping a historic facade safe and intact.When the Plaza reopens, it will carry the same landmark status it has held since 1907, but with a restored exterior designed to protect the building for decades to come. The project is a reminder that even the most celebrated landmarks require periodic, sometimes disruptive, care.
Article Summary: The Plaza Hotel will close in January 2027 and remain shut for at least four years. The New York City Department of Buildings said its most recent inspection found the Plaza’s facade unsafe. The Plaza has closed before, but rarely for this long. From 2005 to 2008, it underwent a $450 million restoration.

Article Title: McClellan Air Force Base closed in 2001; 25 years later, the 3,000-acre Sacramento site has drawn about $600 million in investment, with 10 million sq ft of buildings and a public-use airport
Article Text:
Peacekeeper Gate at McClellan Air Force Base in 1995 (Image Credit: Wikipedia)

From military installation to commercial centre

$600 million investment and millions of square feet

A military airport becomes a public-use facility

Environmental cleanup remains part of the transformation

When McClellan Air Force Base closed in July 2001, the decision threatened thousands of jobs and raised concerns about the economic future of the surrounding Sacramento community. A quarter-century later, the former military installation has become McClellan Park, a business and industrial hub with around $600 million in investment, 10 million square feet of buildings and a public-use airport. According to the U.S. Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC), the redevelopment has involved partnerships between the Air Force, Sacramento County and private developers, alongside environmental restoration. A 2020 McClellan Park fact sheet documents the scale of investment and the site's transformation into a centre for businesses, transport and community services.McClellan Air Force Base was once one of the Sacramento region's major employers. The base supported military logistics and maintenance operations for more than six decades, employing thousands of military and civilian workers. Its closure was announced in 1995 under the federal Base Realignment and Closure process.The decision was expected to cost the local economy thousands of jobs and disrupt businesses that depended on the installation. Before the base officially closed, private businesses were brought into vacant buildings through a process known as a “hot transfer”. This helped retain some employment and allowed redevelopment to begin before the closure, according to McClellan Park’s historical account.The scale of the redevelopment is reflected in the site's infrastructure and commercial activity. McClellan Park's 2020 fact sheet records approximately $600 million in total economic investment, 10 million square feet of buildings and an occupancy rate of 90%. The site accommodates a mix of private businesses, government agencies, industrial facilities, offices and community organisations. Its large buildings have been adapted for different uses, allowing existing structures to serve new commercial purposes instead of requiring every business to start with new construction.The park's development potential also extends beyond its existing buildings. The 2020 fact sheet identifies another five million square feet of potential development, indicating that the property still had room to expand. The same document estimates that the site attracts between 15,000 and 17,000 daily visitors. These figures illustrate how a former military installation has become a major employment and business destination for the surrounding region.One of the most significant changes has been the conversion of the former military airport into a public-use airport serving general aviation. According to McClellan Park's fact sheet, the airport has a 10,600-foot runway. The property also contains seven miles of on-site railway connected directly to Union Pacific and BNSF rail lines, providing transport infrastructure alongside its commercial and industrial facilities.Former military buildings have found new purposes, too. The Air Force officers' club became The Officer's Club restaurant, while the former fitness centre now houses California Family Fitness. A former bowling alley has been converted into a classroom and learning centre operated by Gateway Community Charters. These adaptations demonstrate how existing facilities can support civilian businesses, education, recreation and public services after a military installation closes.The redevelopment has required more than attracting businesses and renovating buildings. Past military operations, waste disposal and chemical spills left soil and groundwater contamination that needed to be addressed.The Air Force has continued environmental restoration alongside the property's transition to civilian use. In 2007, the Air Force and Sacramento County established an agreement designed to accelerate cleanup and allow land to be transferred for redevelopment sooner. The arrangement brought together government agencies, environmental regulators and the private developer. The Air Force Civil Engineer Center reported in 2018 that McClellan's restoration programme had involved 325 sites requiring investigation. Cleanup measures included groundwater treatment, soil remediation and protective caps over contaminated areas. The project also received a US Environmental Protection Agency award recognising efforts to restore former federal facilities for productive reuse.McClellan Park's transformation illustrates how a closed military base can become a long-term economic asset when redevelopment, infrastructure investment and environmental restoration proceed together. Twenty-five years after the base shut down, the Sacramento site continues to serve businesses and the public while demonstrating a different future for land once dedicated to military operations.
Article Summary: McClellan Air Force Base was once one of the Sacramento region's major employers. The base supported military logistics and maintenance operations for more than six decades. Its closure was announced in 1995 under the federal Base Realignment and Closure process. A 2020 McClellan Park fact sheet documents the scale of investment and the site's transformation.

Article Title: Zelenskyy terms Russian peace moves a ‘parody’, slams Trump deal
Article Text:
Zelensky called his EU counterparts “real leaders”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday sharply criticised US President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying it would send cash back to Moscow, and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of reducing peace negotiations to a “parody”.Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy said Russia did not want peace and welcomed the prospect of European allies taking a greater role in talks. EU leaders rallied around him after Trump again criticised Ukraine and called its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”. “And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal,” Zelenskyy said. “This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz . But it will put more money into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”He said Putin was not interested in peace. “He’s playing with words. Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”Zelenskyy called his EU counterparts “real leaders”. “The war will cost 155 billion next year. And we need at least 70 billion more from you – for defence, for weapons,” he said in his address to EU leaders.Building ‘security zone’ in Ukraine, says PutinRussia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along their border, which will be non-negotiable in any future talks with Kyiv, President Putin said Friday. He said the operation was in response to Ukraine’s 2024-25 incursion into Russia’s Kursk region.
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply criticised US President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia. He said it would send cash back to Moscow, and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of reducing peace negotiations to a ‘parody’ Zelenkyy welcomed the prospect of European allies taking a greater role in talks.

Article Title: Order to limit satellite system used by Ukraine came from White House: Report
Article Text:
A Ukrainian drone company, SkyFall, demonstrates StarGate, an aerial medical evacuation drone designed to carry wounded soldiers from front-line positions, potentially saving lives where conventional rescue vehicles cannot reach

Trump didn’t order limits on Kyiv’s SpaceX access: US

Starlink speed not yet fully restored, says Zelensky

NEW YORK/WASHINGTON: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The officials said leaders at the defence department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.President Trump didn’t order any limitations on Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite technology, according to a senior US official.The US official’s comment didn’t preclude the possibility that another US official or agency directed Kyiv’s access be curbed, but it does rebut Zelenskyy’s claim that Trump was responsible.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that Starlink services in his country were still being restored, after partial curbs impeded the military’s ability to defend against Russia. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes,” Zelensky said at a presser in Brussels.
Article Summary: Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that Starlink services in his country were still being restored, after partial curbs impeded the military’s ability to defend against Russia.

Article Title: In 2022, a California owner agreed to a discounted $10 million sale of 402 acres despite approvals for 500+ homes; four years later, a land trust sued to stop permanent roads and utilities inside the
Article Text:
Decades of development pressure

Funding and conservation easement

Legal dispute over infrastructure rights

A conservation group in California has filed a lawsuit to stop plans for permanent roads and utility lines across a newly created 402-acre nature preserve. The legal action comes four years after the land was saved from housing developers. Placer Land Trust filed the lawsuit to block infrastructure construction through Clover Valley, an area of oak woodland and wetlands in Rocklin, California. The group wants to protect the valley floor, which was bought at a reduced price of $10 million in 2022 after years of local opposition to housing projects. The dispute focuses on development rights that were attached to the property before it was protected. Before the land was purchased for conservation, the 402-acre site had full city approvals for more than 500 single-family homes and a major road crossing the valley.Located in western Placer County, Clover Valley is one of the last remaining undeveloped oak woodland areas in the city of Rocklin. For more than 20 years, local residents and environmental groups have campaigned against plans to build housing subdivisions, roads and public infrastructure across the valley floor. The site has important natural and cultural features. Clover Valley Creek flows throughout the year and supports a 20-acre wetland that was partly formed by native beavers.The wetland provides a habitat for threatened bird species, including the California black rail and Swainson's hawk. Archaeological surveys have also found 34 prehistoric Native American sites across the property, including ancient bedrock mortars once used to prepare food. In 2022, the Christian institution Jessup University reached an agreement with the private landowner to buy the 402-acre valley floor for a reduced price of $10 million. This was despite the property having valid approvals for more than 500 homes.To complete the purchase and protect the land for the long term, Jessup University partnered with Placer Land Trust. Early efforts to obtain public conservation grants were delayed by California's state budget deficits. This led to a local fundraising campaign. According to public documents published by Placer Land Trust, the purchase was completed in early 2025 through a joint funding effort. Local government bodies, including Placer County, the Placer County Office of Education, the City of Rocklin and the City of Lincoln, provided financial support. More than $1.3 million was also raised from private donors. Under the agreement, Jessup University owns and manages the land. Placer Land Trust and Placer County jointly hold a permanent conservation easement, a legal agreement that restricts commercial and residential development on the property.Despite the conservation easement being officially recorded, questions have returned over older rights to build infrastructure across the property. Four years after the initial sale agreement was reached, Placer Land Trust began legal proceedings to stop plans for permanent roads and utility lines through the preserve. According to public comments submitted to Placer County, local planning bodies and interest groups have debated whether earlier development approvals allow utility corridors and access roads to cross the valley floor to serve nearby properties. Placer Land Trust argues that allowing permanent utility installations or road construction would directly violate the conservation easement. The group says such work could damage the natural wetlands and historical sites that the agreement was created to protect. The lawsuit asks a court to confirm that the permanent conservation easement takes priority over earlier city development plans. The goal is to ensure that the 402-acre Clover Valley remains protected for nature, education and low-impact recreational activities.
Article Summary: Placer Land Trust filed the lawsuit to block infrastructure construction through Clover Valley, an area of oak woodland and wetlands in Rocklin, California. The group wants to protect the valley floor, which was bought at a reduced price of $10 million in 2022. The dispute focuses on development rights that were attached to the property before it was protected.

Article Title: Five women in Trump’s world who made headlines in last 15 days: Katie Zacharia overtakes Anthony Scaramucci in record of shortest tenure
Article Text:
Five women of Trump world who dominated headlines.

Katie Zacharia

Insiders believe Katie Zacharia was set to fail.

Susie Wiles : The powerful chief of staff facing questions about her own future

Will Susie Wiles be on her way out soon?

Alina Habba : A multimillion-dollar dispute that has turned into a MAGA feud

Alina Habba asks where his billionaire husband's donation vanished.

Kristi Noem quietly moves to her third job

While some lose their jobs in the very first week in the administration, Kristi Noem quietly moves to his third job.

Kimberly Guilfoyle : The ambassador whose tenure ended amid a donor-payment controversy

Kimberly Guilfoyle was shown no mercy because of her past relationship with Donald Trump Jr.

Anthony Scaramucci served as White House communications director for 11 days, from July 21 to July 31, 2017. The record of the shortest tenure in the Trump world is likely to be broken by Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary who was panned on the very first day on the job. Then she appeared on Fox News' Sean Hannity show where she was grilled in such a way that political commentators believed that Hannity must have had the go-ahead from the top because Katie Zacharia was 'set to fail'.Trump announced on October 9 that Zacharia would replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary. She had worked as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security earlier in 2026 and was a senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group. Trump described her as a loyal supporter and a member of the MAGA movement.But the appointment quickly became overshadowed by questions about her professional credentials.Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer and had previously worked at a law firm in Beijing. Her professional profile also listed a general counsel role at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell. Reports suggested that there was no record showing she was registered as an attorney or a member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia.Trump was asked about Zacharia's law practice to which the president did not have any answer, and he turned to Zacharia togive the answer. Zacharia said she practised when she was in China. Turns out, she never passed a bar exam and was never a licensed attorney.By October 16, Trump was publicly suggesting that Zacharia reconsider the position. A White House official said she was being let go from the role. Her tenure had lasted only days.Susie Wiles has occupied one of the most influential positions in Trump's administration, serving as the gatekeeper to the president and a central figure in the operation of the West Wing. But reports of growing internal tensions have put her own position under the spotlight.Wiles, who helped lead Trump's successful 2024 presidential campaign, entered the second administration with a reputation for organisation and discipline. She became the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, a job that involves managing the president's schedule, coordinating senior aides and trying to ensure that the administration's priorities are carried out.Politico reported that Trump was considering replacing Wiles and was reaching out to people asking for names. But officially he dismissed the report calling it fake news and said Susie Wiles will be serving her role for a long time.One source of apparent friction between Trump and Susie Wiles was Trump's decision to approach Zacharia about becoming press secretary without consulting Wiles, according to people familiar with the appointment. The move was viewed internally as undermining the chief of staff and creating uncertainty about who was directing personnel decisions in the West Wing.Wiles has also faced pressure over the outside consulting work of longtime Trump allies Chris LaCivita and Tony Fabrizio Blair, who travelled to Republika Srpska in Bosnia for political consulting work. Trump publicly distanced himself from the two men and threatened to fire them if their work presented a conflict of interest.Wiles has also had a personal health challenge this year. In September, she announced that tests showed no remaining evidence of her breast cancer after treatment, saying she was grateful for the support she had received while continuing to work.Alina Habba, the former personal attorney to Trump, has found herself at the centre of an extraordinary dispute involving a reported multimillion-dollar donation to the Kennedy Center and one of the president's former senior advisers. The controversy became public through an Axios report on October 14, which said Trump had directed White House counsel to examine allegations raised by Habba during a meeting at the White House. Habba reportedly told Trump that a donation her billionaire husband, Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon, intended for the Kennedy Center had not reached the institution.The amount at the centre of the dispute has varied in accounts of the episode. Axios reported that Habba initially cited a figure of $17 million, before the amount in question was narrowed to approximately $5.6 million. White House sources described it as nearly $6 million.The allegation involves Ric Grenell, the former president of the Kennedy Center and a longtime Trump ally. Habba alleged that Grenell had persuaded her husband to include a multimillion-dollar donation in a larger payment linked to a business deal involving a US company. She later discovered, according to the report, that the money did not appear in the Kennedy Center's records.Grenell has strongly denied the allegations. He called them absurd and said he had never asked for money to be sent elsewhere under the pretence that it was a Kennedy Center donation. The White House has sought documentation to support the claims, and an official cautioned that the allegations had not been established and could reflect a misunderstanding.Former DHS secretary Kristi Noem quietly moved to her third job in the Trump administration. After she was fired from her DHS role, she was made a special envoy which expired last month. Now, she will continue working on similar matters, CNN reported. “Kristi Noem’s envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role,” the official said. “She is now a Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio. ”Her ouster in March came after Noem told lawmakers that Trump approved of her agency’s lavish spending on an advertising campaign that prominently showcased her.Noem also filed for divorce from her husband Bryon Noem in September ending their 34 years of marriage.Kimberly Guilfoyle's departure as US ambassador to Greece has become one of the most high-profile personnel controversies involving a Trump ally this month. A former Fox News host and California prosecutor, Guilfoyle was nominated for the diplomatic post after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr ended. She took up a role representing the United States in Athens, where she focused in part on energy cooperation and relations with Greece.But in October, reports about her dealings with a political donor placed her position under pressure. The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle had asked Trump donor Eric Deters to transfer $100,000 to cover her American Express bill before her confirmation hearing. According to the report, the messages suggested she would offer access to administration officials in return. Deters reportedly refused the request.The reporting also raised questions about travel and hospitality. The Wall Street Journal reported allegations involving private flights and luxury accommodation, while Guilfoyle's lawyers said she had followed State Department rules and denied that she had done anything wrong. Her legal team argued that the money she sought related to unpaid fees for speaking engagements that predated her ambassadorial nomination.Trump initially said he was considering whether to fire Guilfoyle. On October 13, the White House announced that she had been asked to resign. She announced her departure within hours, saying the allegations were false and that she intended to vigorously defend her reputation.
Article Summary: Katie Zacharia was panned on the very first day on the job. Susie Wiles is facing questions about her own future as chief of staff. Kristi Noem quietly moves to her third job in the White House. Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure ended amid a donor-payment controversy.

Article Title: 'Don’t trust anybody': Trump's response to Netanyahu question ahead of Israel polls
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump says he “doesn’t trust anybody” in politics when asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while stopping short of committing to an endorsement ahead of Israel’s October 27 election

Iran tensions add to election uncertainty

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he does not trust anyone in politics when asked whether he trusts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as speculation continues over Washington’s role in Israel’s October 27 election.“I don’t trust anybody, honestly,” Trump told right-wing cable news outlet Newsmax. “In the world of politics I don’t trust anybody.”Trump was also asked whether he planned to campaign for Netanyahu, who has frequently highlighted his close relationship with the US president during election campaigns.“Well, they’d like me to be. Yeah, they’d like me to be,” Trump said, referring to Israeli officials who want him to get involved in Netanyahu’s re-election campaign.He nevertheless described his relationship with the Israeli prime minister as “very good” and praised their “very successful… military partnership” against Iran.Trump has repeatedly declined to commit to endorsing Netanyahu ahead of the Israeli election, which comes amid heightened tensions over Iran’s nuclear programme and the possibility of renewed military action.Netanyahu and Trump reportedly discussed the possibility of a joint US-Israeli operation against Iran amid Israeli concerns that Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear programme, according to an Axios report citing US and Israeli officials and other sources familiar with the discussions.The report said Netanyahu had held several calls with Trump over two weeks about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran. The discussions reportedly included possible strikes on Iranian military and nuclear facilities.However, the White House disputed the account, calling the claim that Trump and Netanyahu had discussed resuming the war “false”. A White House official said Trump had made clear that the US would not attack Iran before the American midterm elections.Netanyahu’s office said the Israeli prime minister remained in regular contact with Trump and senior US officials but did not comment on the substance of their conversations.With Israel scheduled to vote on October 27 and US midterm elections approaching, any renewed military campaign against Iran could carry political consequences for both leaders. The prospect of Iranian retaliation has also raised concerns about the potential disruption of Israel’s election process.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump says he ‘doesn’t trust anybody’ in politics when asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump stopped short of committing to an endorsement ahead of Israel’s October 27 election. Netanyahu has frequently highlighted his close relationship with the US president during election campaigns.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

Article Title: ‘Couldn’t wait to kill Indians’: US teen’s neo-Nazi manifesto reveals Hindu temple attack plot
Article Text:
File photo: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, has been charged over an alleged mass shooting plot that may have targeted a Hindu place of worship near Chicago

Planning attack for 2 years

Gun allegedly jammed during visit to temple

Rifle, ammunition and Nazi imagery recovered

Arrest renews concern over anti-Indian hate

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the most effective way to prevent hate-driven attacks? Stronger law enforcement and security Education and awareness against hate Early reporting of extremist threats 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A 19-year-old US man who allegedly told co-workers he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” was arrested over a suspected mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, near Chicago. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack.Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from Palatine, Illinois, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. A judge ordered him detained before trial on Wednesday. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30.According to prosecutors, Paporakis openly identified himself as a white supremacist at work and regularly made disparaging remarks about people of different races, including Indians. His colleagues told investigators that he discussed Nazis and violence and that his behaviour had intensified in the days before his arrest.On Saturday, he allegedly told a co-worker that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and spoke about a plan involving a Hindu temple in Aurora, a city about 65 kilometres southwest of Palatine.He also told a colleague that Sunday would be “a special day”, according to court documents.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis had been planning an attack for about two years, narrowing his focus to a specific location in recent months. He allegedly researched the target using YouTube and Google Street View.Investigators say the material he shared with a co-worker included an eight-page document titled Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto). According to a court document obtained by the Associated Press, the manifesto described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and outlined a plan to kill as many of them as possible.In the document, Paporakis allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”. He also portrayed his outward identity as a working college student as a facade concealing his violent intentions, according to the documents.Police believe Paporakis may have attempted to carry out the attack on Sunday, October 11. Surveillance footage showed his car entering the parking lot of a large Hindu temple in Aurora at around 12.25 pm and leaving approximately 13 minutes later. Investigators said he appeared to be alone in the vehicle.The precise intended target has not been officially identified by police and remains under investigation. The Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora subsequently alerted its members to a security threat, according to The New York Times.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis contacted a co-worker later that day and said his gun had jammed. He reportedly said he had left the scene “super fast” without being seen. He also allegedly sent the colleague a video showing the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to repair it and try again.According to court documents, he told the co-worker that the man he had fired at had been “certainly saved by his God today”. The documents do not establish the identity of the person he allegedly fired at or provide further details about the circumstances.The co-worker contacted police, prompting officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect to locate Paporakis. Investigators believed he might attempt to carry out the plan again, and officers arrested him outside his home on Sunday afternoon.A search of Paporakis’ home uncovered an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and tactical equipment, police and prosecutors said. Investigators also recovered a tactical vest with body armour, items bearing Nazi symbolism and a gas canister labelled with an anti-South Asian slur.The evidence, along with the alleged manifesto and electronic communications, is being examined as part of the investigation. The FBI’s Chicago Field Office assisted local police in reviewing the material.“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” Palatine Police Chief William Nord said, describing the protection of places of worship as a law enforcement priority.Ryan Whalen, the FBI’s Chicago special agent in charge, said the agency worked with local and state authorities to identify and investigate threats driven by extremist ideologies. He credited the rapid response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect police departments with ensuring that the suspect was taken into custody without harm to the community.Paporakis has been charged with making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and unlawful possession of a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, a Class 3 felony. It was not immediately clear whether he had entered a plea or secured legal representation.The case has intensified concerns about hostility towards Indian Americans and other South Asian communities in the United States, particularly as anti-immigration rhetoric and disputes over skilled-worker visas have become increasingly contentious.The FBI does not record crimes against Indian Americans as a separate category. Data on anti-Hindu and anti-Sikh offences therefore offer only a partial picture of the hostility faced by communities whose members often trace their roots to India.Physical attacks and vandalism have also affected Hindu places of worship. In June 2025, between 20 and 30 rounds were reportedly fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside; no injuries were reported. A separate temple in Santa Clara, California, was vandalised later that summer.Online hostility has been more pronounced. A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate found that the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.Researchers have linked some of the hostility to disputes over immigration and the H-1B visa programme, which US employers use to hire skilled foreign workers. Indians receive more than 70% of H-1B visas.The ministry of external affairs also said it was “deeply concerned” by the alleged plot, describing its reported anti-Hindu and racist nature as “particularly disturbing”. Official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal called for a thorough investigation, accountability for those responsible and measures to ensure the safety of the Indian community in the US.
Article Summary: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack. He allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day’

Article Title: Magnitude 7 earthquake strikes Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula
Article Text:
Preliminary info: M7.0 || 123 km SW of #Vilyuchinsk (Russian Federation)​

A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck the Kamchatka Peninsula region of Russia on Friday, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) said, citing seismic data.According to preliminary information shared by EMSC, the earthquake occurred at a depth of 140 km (87 miles), with its epicentre located around 123 km southwest of Vilyuchinsk in Russia’s Far East. The seismic event was recorded at around 3:35 pm local time.The Kamchatka Peninsula, located along the Pacific coast of Russia, is part of the seismically active Pacific Ring of Fire, where tectonic plate movements frequently trigger earthquakes and volcanic activity.The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said there was no tsunami warning, advisory, watch or threat following the earthquake.Further details about the impact of the earthquake, including any reports of damage or casualties, were not immediately available.
Article Summary: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes the Kamchatka Peninsula region of Russia on Friday. Quake occurred at a depth of 140 km (87 miles), with epicentre 123 km southwest of Vilyuchinsk. No tsunami warning, advisory, watch or threat following the earthquake.
