Article Title: France protests flare as PM accuses radical left of exploiting unrest ahead of elections
Article Text:
Student protests are sweeping across France as frustrations rise over overcrowded classrooms and poor school facilities

Why the protests are gaining support

France's student protests have intensified ahead of the 2027 presidential election, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting student anger for electoral gain.According to BBC, thousands of students have taken to the streets over overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school infrastructure and teacher shortages. Trade unions and figures associated with France's Yellow Vest movement are expected to join further demonstrations on Saturday.“Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage,” Lecornu said on Wednesday, accusing the party of encouraging protests while condemning violence.LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has drawn support from demonstrators backing his proposals for a wealth tax, better education and lowering the voting age to 16.The protests come amid mounting pressure on France's public finances and a divided parliament. Economist Anne-Laure Delatte told the BBC that raising taxes could help address the country's debt problem, but warned that such measures would be painful. She also said the European Central Bank could intervene if France's financial difficulties threatened other European economies.The protests have also drawn support from parents who believe demonstrations are necessary to force authorities to address inequality in education.“France likes to speak of égalité, but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit,” three students told the BBC, describing the gap between France’s promise of equality and their experiences.The demonstrations have also revived memories of the May 1968 student movement, which expanded into a major general strike after workers joined the marches.“No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now,” 17-year-old Lola said, reflecting the urgency among young protesters.
Article Summary: Thousands of students have taken to the streets over overcrowded classrooms and poor school facilities. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu accuses the radical- left La France Insoumise of exploiting student anger for electoral gain. Trade unions and figures associated with France's Yellow Vest movement are expected to join further demonstrations on Saturday.

Article Title: US pushes World Bank to scrap oil, gas funding curbs in major energy policy overhaul
Article Text: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has urged the World Bank to end its restrictions on financing upstream oil and gas projects, arguing that developing countries need reliable and affordable energy to drive economic growth, industrialisation and job creation.According to news agency ANI, Bessent made the demand during the October 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, calling for a technology-neutral approach to energy financing and greater support for countries seeking investments in natural gas projects.“The Bank cannot credibly invoke country ownership while categorically excluding upstream projects before their development merits are even assessed,” Bessent said.The demand could reignite debate over the role of fossil fuels in development financing, particularly as developing countries seek to expand electricity access, strengthen energy security and build industrial capacity.The World Bank announced in 2017 that it would stop financing new upstream oil and gas projects after 2019, subject to limited exceptions for upstream natural gas projects in the poorest countries under specific conditions.However, the institution continues to support certain gas-related investments under its broader energy financing framework.Bessent argued that the Bank should prioritise reliable, affordable and abundant energy while directing resources towards countries and projects with the greatest development impact. He welcomed what he described as a shift towards measuring outcomes rather than adhering to arbitrary targets.Bessent highlighted the World Bank and African Development Bank's goal of extending energy access to another 300 million people across the continent, saying that achieving the target would require removing restrictions on natural gas financing and responding to demand for gas projects.The US also welcomed the approval of an International Development Association project aimed at securing near-term gas supplies, preparing midstream and downstream investments, and developing gas strategies in West Africa.Beyond energy policy, Bessent called for reforms to the World Bank's lending framework, including phasing out sovereign lending to countries that have long met the criteria for graduating from Bank support. He cited China and Poland as examples.He also urged the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to accelerate efforts to direct 40 per cent of its new commitments towards the poorest and most fragile countries, saying progress had fallen short.On the IMF, Bessent called for stronger surveillance of global imbalances, debt vulnerabilities and exchange-rate policies, adding that the US would hold the institution accountable for delivering more effective surveillance, lending and debt sustainability assessments.The proposals reflect a broader US push to refocus international financial institutions on economic growth, poverty reduction and development outcomes. Any relaxation of the World Bank's existing restrictions would depend on formal decisions by the institution.
Article Summary: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has urged the World Bank to end its restrictions on financing upstream oil and gas projects. He argued that developing countries need reliable and affordable energy to drive economic growth, industrialisation and job creation. The demand could reignite debate over the role of fossil fuels in development financing, particularly as developing countries seek to expand electricity access.

Article Title: Slick diplomacy: Trump’s crude u-turn on Russia sanctions bails out India
Article Text:
Russian President Putin and US President Trump

TOI correspondent from Washington:

For months, MAGA supremo Donald Trump and his minions threatened to “crush” India’s economy for New Delhi’s purchase of Russian oil. The economics has now caught up with the rhetoric. Faced with soaring fuel prices at home and a widely forecast rout in the mid-term elections, the US President has reversed course and put most of the Russia sanctions on ice, effectively leaving India off the hook for now.The presidential U-turn, announced in an executive order issued on Friday evening (when governments typically drop bad/embarrassing news), invokes the president’s authority to waive provisions of the Graham Act passed last month “in the national interests of the United States.” Among them: 500% tariffs on Russian goods; 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas (which would include India); and 100% tariffs on the top facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.The waiver follows Trump's surprise announcement of a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel fuel, even as his administration has turned on Ukraine to end a war that began with Russia's invasion. The deadline to implement the sanctions was to expire on Sunday, one month from the day the bill was passed.This does not mean sanctions threat has disappeared. The executive order leaves the administration room to reverse course if Trump or designated officials later decide that further action is appropriate. In theory, the president retains leverage; in practice though, a threat that is announced, legislated, signed and then shelved risks becoming less an instrument of coercion than a negotiating prop.For India, which faced the prospect of tariffs as high as 100 per cent on goods entering the American market under the legislation, the reprieve is welcome -- and well may it send a bill to Washington for economic advice rendered. New Delhi repeatedly insisted that its energy purchases are governed by market conditions, supply security and affordability -- the very argument now being made by Washington. It also maintained steadfastly that its energy decisions cannot simply be dictated by the political preferences of Western capitals.While the presidential order is admirably concise about the legal manoeuvre, it is considerably less forthcoming about the political embarrassment and diplomatic debacle -- arising mainly from the vituperative hectoring the bill’s authors subjected India to. “If you keep buying cheap Russian oil… we will tariff the hell out of you and we're going to crush your economy,” raged the late Senator Lindsay Graham, who piloted the legislation, warning of tariffs up to 500 per cent. India survived; Graham did not, passing away on July 11 at 71.Graham’s Democratic co-sponsor Richard Blumenthal was scarcely more restrained. “To China and India: You better clean up your act. Buy your oil and gas somewhere else. Appeasement is not a strategy,” he declared. On Friday, Blumenthal was left fuming at Trump’s appeasement, accusing him of standing “on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia’s war machine.”Forgotten amid the hand-wringing: The Biden administration tacitly encouraged--and explicitly permitted -- India to purchase Russian oil to stabilize global energy supply so long as those purchases adhered to the price cap mechanism. Now, with Graham gone but his legislation very much alive, Trump has discovered that appeasement may not be a strategy either -- but neither is making American motorists pay a premium for geopolitical virtue.For India, the reprieve is reason enough for a quiet celebration. It was not exactly a Taco Tuesday, but it was certainly a Samosa Saturday in New Delhi: the country Trump threatened to crush for buying cheap Russian oil has been let off the hook by a president who has now discovered the virtues of affordable energy. The oil hasn’t changed, nor has the argument. Only Washington’s position has.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has reversed course and put most of the Russia sanctions on ice. U-turn follows Trump's surprise announcement of a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel fuel. The deadline to implement the sanctions was to expire on Sunday, one month from the day the bill was passed.

Article Title: A Wyoming ranch grew from a 160-acre homestead into a 320-acre dude ranch; its owners sold it to the National Park Service with a lifetime estate agreement
Article Text:
Representative Image of a historic American West ranch featuring cowboy culture and rustic log cabins ( AI Generrated Image)

White Grass Ranch history: how a homestead became a dude ranch

Bar BC Ranches , Inc. and the White Grass Ranch for Boys

Frank Galey and the lifetime estate agreement

From guest ranch to historic preservation training centre

Long before Grand Teton National Park became a major destination for visitors, White Grass Ranch in Wyoming’s Jackson Hole valley was part of a growing industry built around the American West’s landscapes and ranching traditions. According to the National Park Service (NPS), Harold Hammond filed a 160-acre homestead claim in 1913. His partner, George Tucker Bispham, later developed an adjoining claim, and the two properties eventually formed a 320-acre ranch. By around 1919, White Grass was accommodating paying guests, initially in three log houses. Activities associated with the ranch included horseback riding, swimming and fishing, while its library and card room offered indoor recreation. In 1956, Frank Galey and his wife, Inge, sold the ranch to the NPS while reserving a lifetime estate that allowed the family to continue using the property for residential and guest-ranch purposes. After the ranch’s guest operation ended in 1985, its historic buildings were eventually rehabilitated for a different purpose: training people to preserve historic structures.Dude ranching developed as cattle ranchers began welcoming paying guests who wanted to experience the Western lifestyle.The NPS’s account of dude ranching in Grand Teton National Park describes how ranches in Jackson Hole evolved to accommodate visitors while retaining elements of their agricultural operations. Rather than working as full-time ranch hands, guests could experience activities associated with ranch life in a setting shaped by mountains, open land and livestock.White Grass began as a homestead rather than a purpose-built tourist facility. In 1913, Hammond filed a claim for 160 acres in the Teton National Forest area. A log structure was built on the property that year, although the length of time Hammond lived in the Main Cabin is unclear. Bispham started improving adjoining land in 1915 and later established his own homestead there. Their separate claims received patents in 1920 and 1923, respectively, according to the NPS’s White Grass Ranch cultural landscape history. The partners developed the property gradually. By around 1919, they were accommodating guests in three log houses. White Grass subsequently became the third dude ranch established in what is now Grand Teton National Park. The ranch’s early development illustrates how homesteads in Jackson Hole could evolve from agricultural properties into businesses catering to visitors seeking recreation and an experience of Western ranch life.White Grass underwent a major change in ownership and use during the 1920s. Between 1923 and 1928, Hammond and Bispham transferred their claims to Bar BC Ranches, Inc., a partnership that included the two men as well as Struthers Burt, Horace Carncross, Irving Corse and Sinclair Armstrong. Burt and Carncross were founders of the Bar BC Ranch, linking White Grass’s ownership history to the wider dude-ranch industry in Jackson Hole. During this period, White Grass became known as the White Grass Ranch for Boys. Thirteen cabins were added to the three already in existence, and a concrete swimming pool was built in a hayfield. Young men, including visitors from eastern universities, spent parts of the summer learning traditional ranch skills and elements of self-reliance, according to the NPS.In 1928, Hammond and Bispham ended their partnership with Bar BC Ranches, Inc., and Hammond purchased the property, buildings and furnishings from Bispham. Hammond continued operating the 320-acre ranch over the following decade, combining guest accommodation with agricultural work. The NPS records that the ranch supported about 50 head of cattle under a grazing lease and that its operations included irrigation and haymaking. A separate bathhouse was also built, and bathrooms were later added to some guest cabins. These changes show that White Grass was not simply a holiday destination. Its operation continued to depend on the land, livestock and agricultural infrastructure that had shaped its early development.According to the National Park Service, Hammond died in 1939, after which his stepson, Frank Galey, took over management of White Grass Ranch. The business was interrupted by the Second World War, when the ranch nearly shut down. Galey returned in 1946 and operated White Grass until his death in July 1985. The NPS describes it as the longest-lived active dude ranch in Jackson Hole. According to the National Park Service, Frank and Inge Galey sold White Grass Ranch to the agency in 1956 while reserving a lifetime estate agreement permitting continued family use of the property for residential and guest-ranch purposes. The arrangement meant that the federal government acquired the ranch while the family retained the right to use it during the lifetime-estate period. The ranch continued operating as a dude ranch until 1985, when Galey’s death brought the operation to an end and the lifetime estate expired.The National Park Service’s historical account states that, after Galey’s death, his second wife, Nora, hired an auctioneer to sell the ranch’s business assets. The park subsequently considered how to manage the property. During the late 1980s and early 1990s, several cabins were sold, water features and ranch fencing were removed, and the remaining buildings were boarded up as the initial management approach sought to return the site towards its natural condition.White Grass Ranch later acquired a new role in conservation. In 2003, the National Park Service and the National Trust for Historic Preservation entered into an agreement to rehabilitate the historic ranch for use as a regional training centre. Preservation work began in 2005 and included repairs to foundations, roofs, windows and doors, the replacement of deteriorated logs, and improvements to ageing utility systems. The National Park Service announced the rehabilitation’s completion in December 2016, following 11 years of preservation work. According to the NPS announcement, White Grass became the home and primary training centre of the National Park Service’s Western Center for Historic Preservation. The site’s historic buildings now support training in techniques used to preserve traditional structures, including log buildings.The NPS and the National Trust jointly funded the rehabilitation, which cost approximately $3 million. The completed project adapted the surviving ranch buildings for a new use while retaining their historic character. Sleeping cabins provide accommodation for trainees, while the Main, Hammond and Bath House cabins serve as shared spaces for meals, teaching and practical work. According to the National Park Service, the White Grass Heritage Project was established in 2014 to collect oral histories, documents and photographs about life at the ranch. Former guests and wranglers have been invited to contribute their memories, preserving accounts of a business that operated for decades before closing in 1985. White Grass Ranch’s history reflects two different periods in Jackson Hole’s development. It began with homestead claims and agricultural work, grew into a dude ranch that welcomed visitors seeking a taste of Western life, and eventually became a site for teaching historic preservation. Its buildings remain part of the landscape, but their purpose has changed from accommodating holiday guests to helping protect historic structures elsewhere.
Article Summary: White Grass Ranch in Wyoming was part of a growing industry built around the American West’s landscapes and ranching traditions. In 1913, Harold Hammond filed a claim for 160 acres in the Teton National Forest area. By around 1919, White Grass was accommodating paying guests, initially in three log houses. Activities associated with the ranch included horseback riding, swimming and fishing. In 1956, Frank Galey and his wife, Inge, sold the ranch to the NPS while reserving a lifetime estate that allowed the family to continue using the property for residential and guest-ranch purposes.

Article Title: In 1993, a rancher donated 300 American bison that were released on an Oklahoma prairie; today, more than 2,000 roam the preserve, helping restore one of Earth's most threatened ecosystems
Article Text:
From 300 bison to a herd of thousands

How bison help restore the grassland

Why controlled fires are essential

Research shows how bison can increase plant diversity

Protecting one of America's most threatened ecosystems

In 1993, Oklahoma ranchers Kenneth and Dianna Adams donated 300 American bison to The Nature Conservancy, setting in motion a conservation effort to restore one of North America's most threatened ecosystems. More than three decades later, the herd has grown to thousands of animals roaming the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve near Pawhuska, Oklahoma. Spanning 39,650 acres, the preserve protects a rare stretch of native grassland where bison grazing and carefully managed fires help maintain the natural balance of the prairie. The animals influence the growth of native plants, create habitats for other species and help preserve the ecological processes that shaped the Great Plains for thousands of years. Their return is particularly significant because less than 4% of the original tallgrass prairie remains.The bison were named the Christina Adams Bison Herd after the ranchers' daughter. Their growing population has become a defining feature of the preserve, where the animals roam across open grassland and graze among native vegetation.The conservation effort also demonstrates how restoring a native species can contribute to the protection of an entire landscape.The preserve supports hundreds of plant and animal species, making the long-term management of its grasslands important for biodiversity.The original herd arrived in autumn 1993, when the Adams family donated the animals from their Ken-Ada Ranch. The Nature Conservancy had begun assembling the preserve through land acquisitions in 1989, with the goal of protecting and restoring the region's disappearing tallgrass prairie.The herd has since expanded considerably. The Nature Conservancy has reported around 2,700 bison during summer, including calves born that year, with numbers falling after the annual autumn roundup. The animals are managed as part of the preserve's conservation programme, which combines wildlife management with efforts to maintain the grassland's natural character.The preserve covers approximately 39,650 acres and is recognised as the largest protected remnant of tallgrass prairie in the world. Its landscape includes rolling grasslands, native wildflowers, scattered trees and waterways, offering a glimpse of an ecosystem that once covered vast areas of central North America.Bison play a central role in shaping the prairie through their feeding habits and movement. They primarily graze on grasses, influencing which plants dominate the landscape and creating opportunities for other vegetation to grow. This helps maintain a varied grassland rather than allowing a limited number of plant species to dominate every area.Their activities also affect the soil. As bison move through the preserve, they disturb patches of ground, redistribute nutrients through their waste and create depressions known as wallows by rolling in the soil. These shallow hollows can collect rainwater and provide small habitats for insects and other wildlife.The resulting variation in vegetation and ground conditions supports a wider range of organisms. Native grasses and flowering plants provide food and shelter for insects, while birds and mammals depend on the different habitats found across the prairie.Bison grazing is combined with prescribed burning, another important tool in tallgrass prairie management. Without periodic disturbance, woody plants can spread into open grasslands, gradually changing the landscape and reducing the habitat available to species adapted to prairie conditions.The Nature Conservancy uses a patch-burn approach, setting controlled fires in different sections of the preserve at different times. Recently burned areas produce fresh vegetation, while other sections retain older grasses and provide different feeding opportunities for wildlife.Bison graze across these contrasting areas, further shaping plant growth and maintaining a changing mosaic of habitats. Together, grazing and fire recreate some of the natural processes that historically sustained the Great Plains, helping keep the preserve an open grassland rather than allowing it to become dominated by shrubs and trees.The ecological importance of bison is also supported by long-term research at the Konza Prairie Biological Station in Kansas. A study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in August 2022 examined nearly three decades of vegetation data from areas grazed by bison, areas grazed by cattle and areas without large grazers.Researchers found that native plant species richness was 103% higher at the small-plot scale and 86% higher at the larger catchment scale in bison-grazed areas than in ungrazed areas. Cattle grazing also increased plant richness, although the gains were smaller.The research highlighted how grazing by native large herbivores can influence the composition of grassland vegetation over long periods. The study also found that the gains associated with bison grazing persisted through a period that included severe drought, underscoring the importance of grazing patterns in maintaining prairie biodiversity.Tallgrass prairie once stretched across 14 US states, extending from Texas to Minnesota and into parts of Canada. Agricultural conversion and urban development have destroyed much of this habitat, leaving less than 4% of its original extent. Much of the remaining prairie is concentrated in Oklahoma and Kansas, particularly in the Flint Hills region.The Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve protects a significant part of this surviving landscape. It supports more than 700 plant species, over 300 bird species and around 80 mammal species, according to The Nature Conservancy. Its grasslands provide food, shelter and breeding habitat for wildlife while preserving native vegetation that has disappeared from much of the region.The return of the bison has helped restore a defining feature of the prairie. More than 30 years after the original donation, the herd remains central to the preserve's conservation work, showing how native wildlife and careful land management can help sustain a threatened ecosystem for future generations.
Article Summary: Oklahoma ranchers donated 300 American bison to The Nature Conservancy in 1993. More than three decades later, the herd has grown to thousands of animals roaming the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve near Pawhuska, Oklahoma. Spanning 39,650 acres, the preserve protects a rare stretch of native grassland where bison grazing and carefully managed fires help maintain the natural balance of the prairie.

Article Title: Washington parents built a hidden fairy garden between bookshelves for their daughters, filled with miniature trees and glowing stars
Article Text:
Melissa Miller’s daughter looking in the library fairy garden. Image Credit: PEOPLE/Melissa Miller

How did Washington parents create a hidden fairy garden for their daughters

A childhood dream found a place in the family home

What makes the miniature forest special

The glowing stars honour a much-loved family member

Small figures reflect the daughters' individual personalities

A home filled with imaginative surprises

A couple in Washington has turned an unused corner of their home library into a hidden fairy garden, creating a special place filled with miniature trees, glowing stars and personal touches for their two young daughters. Melissa Miller, 41, and her husband, Aaron Miller, 38, designed the secret space to bring a little magic into their children's everyday lives. As reported by PEOPLE in an exclusive article published in August 2026, the project also reflects the couple's love of imaginative spaces and the importance of family memories.The idea began when the Millers moved into their home and discussed how to arrange the space for their family. According to PEOPLE, they asked their daughters, aged four and a half and eight, whether they would prefer separate bedrooms or a shared room alongside a family library. The girls chose the library, giving their parents an opportunity to create a reading space that would also encourage imagination.While Aaron was building the library, the couple noticed an empty area beneath some shelves in one corner. Rather than covering it completely, they decided to keep the space accessible for a future surprise.Melissa, who had loved stories about magical lands, hidden rooms and secret passages since childhood, felt that a fairy garden would suit the library's garden-inspired theme.The construction of the library took several months. However, the hidden garden did not take shape immediately. Melissa became occupied with another creative project, a dollhouse built into the wall, and temporarily forgot about the small corner she had set aside.Melissa eventually returned to the idea about two years after first discussing it with Aaron. As PEOPLE reports, she began making miniature trees and planning a tiny forest with a clearing where fairies could gather for a picnic.Her original plan was to complete the garden herself and let both daughters discover it when it was ready. However, her younger daughter was at home with her during the day, so Melissa eventually invited her to help with the surprise.The little girl was delighted to take part and enjoyed helping create something that her older sister could discover later. The project consequently became more than a decorative addition to the library. It also gave mother and daughter an opportunity to work together on a shared creative activity.Melissa's idea was closely connected to her own childhood wishes. She had always wanted to encounter something magical unexpectedly, rather than simply reading about it in a book. Creating a secret world inside her home allowed her to turn that long-held dream into something her daughters could experience themselves.The fairy garden's details were carefully made by hand. PEOPLE reports that Melissa used air-dry clay, paint and leftover artificial flowers and leaves from earlier projects to create several of the miniature trees. These materials helped her build a tiny woodland scene within the limited space beneath the bookshelves.The design includes a small clearing intended for a fairy picnic, bringing the idea of an enchanted forest into a compact corner of the library. The setting also features glowing stars, a moon and a little comet, adding a night-sky effect to the miniature landscape.One of the most difficult parts of the project was painting the inside of the awkwardly shaped space. Melissa told PEOPLE that reaching into the corner made the task particularly challenging. Nevertheless, she continued working until the scene was complete.The finished garden combines handmade decorations with elements chosen specifically for the family, making it different from a standard miniature display. Each detail contributes to a small world that reflects the children's interests and their parents' efforts to make the home feel full of surprises.Beyond its playful appearance, the fairy garden holds a deeply personal meaning for the Millers. The couple included details in memory of their son, Luke, who was stillborn in 2020.In her interview with PEOPLE, Melissa explained that the moon, stars and comet were added to remember him. Following Luke's death, the family spent considerable time healing and camping in nature. The summer of his death coincided with the appearance of Comet Neowise, which became a lasting reminder of him.The celestial decorations therefore serve a purpose beyond making the miniature forest look magical. They connect the family's experience of loss with memories of time spent outdoors and the process of healing together.By incorporating these elements into a place designed for their daughters, Melissa and Aaron created a space that brings together childhood wonder, family history and remembrance. The garden's meaning is personal, yet it remains part of an everyday setting where the girls can explore and play.The miniature characters also have personal connections. According to PEOPLE, a fairy sitting with an open book represents the older daughter, who enjoys reading and has a strong interest in learning and imaginative play. Melissa also described her interests in nature, gardening, animals, swimming and camping.The younger daughter is represented by a fairy on a swing, reflecting her love of swinging, jumping, art and creating little homes for her tiny toys. Her enthusiasm for helping with the garden made the figure especially fitting.Even the family's cat, Blossom, has a place in the miniature forest. Melissa added a small white cat with blue eyes to resemble the family's pet.These details make the display a reflection of the household rather than simply a decorative fairy scene. Each figure gives the girls something familiar to discover, while the hidden location adds another layer of excitement.The fairy garden is only one of several unusual features the Millers have created. PEOPLE reports that the family also has a Mouse House, a two-sided dollhouse built into a wall that opens into two different rooms. It includes electricity, tiny light switches and a working doorbell.Aaron has also built a saltwater fish tank into the living room wall, while the house features a secret passageway, fulfilling another of Melissa's childhood ambitions.
Article Summary: Melissa Miller, 41, and her husband, Aaron Miller, 38, designed the secret space to bring a little magic into their children's everyday lives. The couple included details in memory of their son, Luke, who was stillborn in 2020. The garden combines handmade decorations with elements chosen specifically for the family.

Article Title: 'Broad, troubling trend': US lawmakers urge FBI probe into mass shooting plot at Illinois Hindu temple
Article Text:
US lawmakers press FBI to probe alleged plot against Illinois Hindu temple

The US Congressional Caucus on India has urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois as a federal hate crime. IIn a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday, the caucus called for a thorough probe to determine whether anyone encouraged, assisted or coordinated with the 19-year-old suspect, either online or offline.“This plot did not emerge in isolation but reflects broader, troubling trends,” Congressmen Rich McCormick and Ro Khanna, co-chairs of the House India Caucus, said in the letter.The letter cited FBI data showing an increase in reported hate crimes targeting Sikh, Hindu and Buddhist communities in 2025. The lawmakers urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot as a potential federal hate crime and bring all charges supported by the evidence.They also called on the agencies to “share timely threat information with state and local law enforcement and with Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras, and other South Asian houses of worship, and offer them protective resources”.The lawmakers further asked Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel to brief the caucus on threats facing Hindu and Indian Americans and the steps being taken by their agencies to address them.“Brief the Caucus on threats facing Hindu Americans and Indian Americans and the steps the Department and FBI are taking to address them,” they said.US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi earlier said he and his family were worshipping at the Hindu temple in Aurora when the alleged attack was attempted. “My family and I were worshipping at our Hindu temple in Aurora on Sunday when a white supremacist attempted a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans. I'm grateful to those who helped prevent a tragedy, but we must come together to confront the hatred that put so many innocent lives at risk,” he said.The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Friday also expressed deep concern over the incident. Addressing a media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “This is obviously a matter of deep concern for us. At the same time, it is something that shows or highlights the increasing cases of hate crimes and racial discrimination against the Indian communities in the United States.”Jaiswal said India had taken note of the action taken by US law enforcement authorities following the incident, but called on Washington to ensure the safety and security of Indian nationals in the country.The accused was arrested on October 11 after a colleague alerted authorities to suspicious electronic communications, according to investigators and local police departments.Investigators later recovered a document outlining the alleged attack plan, along with firearms, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition, tactical equipment, body armour and a manifesto titled “Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter's Manifesto)”, which expressed white supremacist views.Prosecutors alleged that the accused openly identified as a white supremacist and expressed an eagerness to kill Indian people. The allegations remain subject to judicial proceedings and have not been proven in court.
Article Summary: US Congressional Caucus on India has urged the FBI and the Department of Justice to investigate the alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois as a federal hate crime. The caucus called for a thorough probe to determine whether anyone encouraged, assisted or coordinated with the 19-year- old suspect, either online or offline.

Article Title: 'Prioritize rights & freedoms when you meet Indian officials': US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio amid anti-SIR stir
Article Text:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio

Jayapal reiterates call for freedom of expression

Student protests and voter roll revision flagged

US lawmakers seek probe into demonstrations

India rejects Jayapal's remarks

US lawmakers have urged secretary of state Marco Rubio to raise concerns over democratic freedoms with Indian officials during his upcoming visit.In a letter dated October 16, six US lawmakers, including Pramila Jayapal and James P McGovern, have urged Rubio to discuss freedom of expression, the right to protest and voting rights with Indian officials. They also raised concerns over student protests following exam-related issues and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The lawmakers also noted steps taken by the government to address students' concerns, including education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.Jayapal shared the appeal in a post on X on Friday (local time), stressing the responsibility of both countries to uphold democratic freedoms. “As the world’s largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression.”“@RepMcGovern and I are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to prioritize those freedoms and human rights when he meets with Indian officials in the coming days,” she added.The letter was signed by Jayapal, McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Chuy Garcia, Eleanor Holmes Norton and Ilhan Omar.It highlighted the importance of democratic principles in relations between the two countries.“As the world’s largest democracies and state parties to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression,” the letter stated.The lawmakers referred to protests following the leak and cancellation of the national medical college entrance examination. They also raised concerns over demonstrations linked to the Election Commission's SIR exercise.Citing concerns raised by UN human rights experts, the letter questioned the transparency of the voter roll revision process and its potential implications for electoral participation. It also referred to reports of protest-related detentions and the response of law enforcement agencies to demonstrations.The lawmakers acknowledged the Indian government's response to student grievances following examination-related concerns.“We note that the Indian government has taken some steps to address the grievances of students impacted by exam leaks, with the notable inclusion of Education Minister Pradhan’s resignation,” the letter stated.The letter also referred to reports that individuals associated with Indian diplomatic missions had photographed participants at demonstrations in Washington, Chicago and San Francisco. The lawmakers called for the reports to be investigated.They urged the US administration to encourage transparent investigations into alleged violations linked to law enforcement actions during protests, review detentions involving the exercise of fundamental freedoms and examine the reports concerning demonstrations in the United States.“The free exercise of fundamental freedoms and the right to vote is core to the democratic identities of both the United States and India,” the letter stated.The lawmakers called on Rubio to raise these issues during his meetings with Indian officials.The appeal comes after India strongly criticised Jayapal's comments on its electoral process on Friday, describing them as "unwarranted, uninformed" and tantamount to interference in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy.Responding to a question during a bi-weekly media briefing in New Delhi, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, "We find the remarks of the Congresswoman unwarranted and uninformed and tantamount to interfering in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy. This is an approach that undermines democracy itself."Earlier, on Thursday, India's Ambassador to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra, had also rejected Jayapal's allegations regarding a voter purge.Describing her remarks as "unacceptable interference in India's internal affairs", Kwatra wrote on X, "The remarks by Rep. Jayapal on India's electoral and political processes are unacceptable interference in India's internal affairs."He added, "India is a vibrant democracy with robust, independent constitutional institutions and a longstanding record of free and fair elections. Always open to constructive conversation with the Congresswoman to dispel her misconceptions."Rubio is scheduled to visit India and Uzbekistan between October 17 and 22. His India itinerary includes Mumbai and Jamnagar, where he is expected to meet senior Indian government officials to strengthen the bilateral strategic partnership and explore enhanced energy cooperation.Meanwhile, the ECI is conducting a nationwide Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in multiple phases. The Commission has clarified that lists identifying absent, shifted, deceased and duplicate voters were publicly displayed and shared with political parties. It has also maintained that people whose names have been deleted from the electoral rolls can apply for enrolment at any time.
Article Summary: US lawmakers urge Rubio to raise concerns over democratic freedoms with Indian officials during his upcoming visit. They also raised concerns over student protests following exam-related issues and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. India strongly criticised Jayapal's comments on its electoral process on Friday, describing them as "unwarranted, uninformed" and tantamount to interference.

Article Title: 'Threw phone at him, fought him': How teacher, armed father tackled Oregon gunman who killed 4
Article Text:
​ A drone view shows a vehicle belonging to a bystander who fatally shot the suspect (Reuters)​​

A teacher and an armed father stopped the teenage gunman who opened fire at an Oregon elementary school, killing three children and a teacher, as police investigate the motive behind the attack.According to Reuters, Police chief Mike Krantz said the teacher threw her cellphone at the gunman before tackling him and attempting to disarm him.An armed father, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, then entered the classroom and shot the teenager, killing him before police arrived. Krantz said the actions of both individuals likely prevented further casualties.Kaylub Giamanco’s mother, Kenda Freeman, said her son was not seeking recognition for his actions and expressed gratitude to the first responders, school staff and community members who helped after the shooting. The family requested privacy as they dealt with the aftermath of the incident, particularly for Giamanco’s two daughters who attend the school.Bend Police chief Mike Krantz praised the teacher for confronting the gunman and fighting to protect the children inside the classroom. He said her actions likely prevented further casualties, describing her intervention as an act of courage during an extremely dangerous situation.The shooting took place on October 15 at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. The gunman, identified as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, was a former student at the school.Three children aged five, eight and 11, along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert, were killed, while a seven-year-old child and another teacher were injured.Police said the teenager fired at a truck outside the school before throwing his shotgun over a fence, climbing after it and entering the building through locked glass doors. He then opened fire inside the classroom, firing at least 15 rounds, according to investigators.Authorities are continuing to investigate the motive behind the attack and how the teenager obtained the firearm.
Article Summary: The shooting took place on October 15 at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. The gunman, identified as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, was a former student at the school. Three children aged five, eight and 11, along with teacher Meghan Lambert, 25, were killed, while a seven year-old child and another teacher were injured.

Article Title: Tony Hawk founded a nonprofit in 2002 to expand access to free public skateparks; it has since helped fund nearly 700 parks across all 50 US states
Article Text:
Representative Image of young skateboarders enjoying free access to a vibrant public skatepark ( AI Generrated Image)

The Skatepark Project: how Tony Hawk’s foundation began in 2002

Who Wants to Be a Millionaire

Free skateparks in underserved communities: how grants and local funding work

Los Angeles skate plaza: a $70,000 donation accepted in 2026

For young skateboarders, finding a safe, legal place to practise is not always easy. Since 2002, a nonprofit founded by professional skateboarder Tony Hawk has helped communities develop public skateparks, particularly in areas with limited recreational facilities. Formerly known as the Tony Hawk Foundation, the organisation became The Skatepark Project in 2020 to put its mission at the centre of its identity. It provides grants, technical assistance and other resources to communities seeking to create free public skating spaces. The organisation says it has helped fund nearly 700 skateparks across all 50 US states. A February 2026 Los Angeles City Council report separately documents its involvement in a skateboarding facility at the West Los Angeles Municipal Complex. Its work includes permanent community parks and temporary facilities developed with municipal authorities. Examples from Augusta, Kansas, and Los Angeles show how nonprofit support can help expand access to public recreation.Hawk established the nonprofit to address the shortage of public places where young people could skateboard legally. According to The Skatepark Project’s account, Hawk used the $125,000 he won onin 2001 to help launch the organisation. It was formally founded in 2002 as the Tony Hawk Foundation.The foundation focused on helping communities secure funding and other resources for public skateparks, especially in underserved areas. Rather than limiting its work to financial assistance, it developed a community-oriented approach involving local advocates, public authorities and skatepark users.In 2020, the foundation adopted the name The Skatepark Project. A 2020 announcement about the rebranding reported that the organisation had helped fund more than 600 public skateparks across all 50 states. Its current programmes include grants of up to $25,000 for eligible projects, as well as technical assistance and support for youth activities. The organisation’s grant guidelines specify that projects must provide permanent, public concrete skateparks in underserved communities, remain free to use and involve local users in planning, fundraising and design. The organisation’s grant guidelines also set requirements for community support and project funding.The emphasis on free access is central to the organisation’s mission. A public skatepark does not require users to pay an entry fee or purchase a membership, although skaters may still need their own equipment. The Skatepark Project’s support is intended to help communities create facilities where young people can participate without the cost of private recreational venues. One of its regional initiatives is Built to Play, a partnership with the Ralph C. Wilson, Jr. Foundation. The Built to Play initiative, a partnership with the Ralph C. Wilson, Jr. Foundation, aimed to support up to 20 public skateparks across 16 counties in Southeast Michigan and Western New York. A separate example comes from Augusta, Kansas. In an announcement about a $15,000 grant from The Skatepark Project, the city said the funding would help address potential construction-cost increases for its community skatepark. The city also described plans to pursue additional funding and continue local fundraising.The Augusta project subsequently opened to the public on 5 November 2023, according to the city’s skatepark opening announcement. The example illustrates the wider role of municipal planning and community investment in establishing public recreational facilities. The Built to Play initiative and Augusta’s grant are separate examples of the organisation’s work, rather than parts of the same programme. The organisation’s reported national reach should be distinguished from estimates of park usage. Published figures for annual visits vary, and the available material does not establish whether they use comparable dates or counting methods. These estimates should therefore not be presented as a verified count of unique visitors.The organisation’s work also includes temporary facilities developed with local authorities. In Los Angeles, the City Council considered a donation valued at approximately $70,000 for skateboarding features at the West Los Angeles Municipal Complex. The city’s official council record confirms that the council adopted the Government Operations Committee report on 3 February 2026, with all recorded votes in favour. The donation comprised labour, materials and equipment for four skate obstacles, handrails, ledges, a wedge spine, signage and replicas of courthouse monuments.Under the proposal, the Skatepark Project would oversee the design and construction with professional builders and cover the associated costs. The improvements were intended to provide a temporary skating facility while the complex remained subject to redevelopment plans. A local report described new features and murals being unveiled at the site on 3 February 2026, the same day the City Council adopted the committee report. The Los Angeles example shows that the organisation’s role can extend beyond conventional grants. It can contribute equipment, construction resources and project oversight to help create skating opportunities at existing public sites.Across its programmes, The Skatepark Project combines grant funding, technical assistance and partnerships with communities and public agencies. Its reported national reach provides a measure of the scale of its work, while local examples show how individual facilities depend on planning, funding and construction. The number of parks alone cannot establish how much access has improved in every community, but the projects demonstrate a sustained effort to make public skateboarding spaces available without entry fees.
Article Summary: The Skatepark Project provides grants, technical assistance and other resources to communities seeking to create free public skating spaces. The organisation says it has helped fund nearly 700 skateparks across all 50 US states. Examples from Augusta, Kansas, and Los Angeles show how nonprofit support can help expand access to public recreation.

Article Title: 'When in doubt, say Mohammad': Trump jokes about common Middle East name while taking aim at Iran
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump jokes about the popularity of the name Mohammad while mocking Iran’s presidency at a campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections (File photo)

US President Donald Trump joked about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world while taking aim at Iran's presidency during a campaign rally in Georgia on Friday."You know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" news agency Reuters quoted Trump saying during a campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it for years now. I've never been wrong." The crowd in Georgia gave the joke a muted response.Trump made the remarks while discussing Iran at a rally held in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections."Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, before pretending to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian has been Iran's president since 2024.Mohammad is among the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.Trump's remarks come amid repeated criticism from rights advocates and Muslim advocacy groups over what they describe as rhetoric that mocks or demonises Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.During the midterm campaign season, Trump has intensified his rhetoric against Somali and Muslim Americans, including Muslim Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, who came to the US as a Somali refugee.Trump also reiterated his vow that Iran would never obtain a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war against Tehran aimed, in part, at crippling its nuclear programme.An annual report released earlier this year by the Council on American-Islamic Relations attributed a rise in Islamophobia in the US partly to Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump joked about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world. He also took aim at Iran's presidency during a campaign rally in Georgia on Friday. Mohammad is among the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Article Title: Trump’s Truth Social loses 30% traffic as US midterms nears
Article Text:
Truth Social averaged around 260,000 daily users last month, down from a peak of 420,000 in June 2025

US President Donald Trump’s social media platform Truth Social has witnessed a sharp decline in traffic over the past year, with digital intelligence data from Similarweb showing a drop of more than 30%.Despite Trump’s frequent posts on the platform, daily traffic has fallen significantly from its earlier peak. Truth Social averaged around 260,000 daily users last month, down from a peak of 420,000 in June 2025, according to Similarweb data cited in The Independent report.Trump is known for posting frequently on Truth Social, often sharing a flurry of updates within hours. On October 14, he reportedly shared around 25 posts in a matter of hours, including a video depicting him wrestling with a tiger.The decline in traffic comes as the platform struggles to keep pace with larger social media networks. The figures also raise questions about Truth Social’s ability to sustain user engagement despite its prominent association with the US president.Trump launched Truth Social after Twitter, now known as X, banned him on January 8, 2021, following the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. Trump Media & Technology Group subsequently launched the platform in February 2022.The group in May reported more than $405 million in first-quarter net losses this year.
Article Summary: Truth Social averaged around 260,000 daily users last month, down from a peak of 420,000 in June 2025. The decline in traffic comes as the platform struggles to keep pace with larger social media networks. Trump is known for posting frequently on Truth Social, often sharing a flurry of updates within hours.

Article Title: A 37-centimetre Qianlong vase appeared in a Cornish property brochure; it later sold at Sotheby’s for £304,800
Article Text:
Image: Sotheby’s

The genuine Qianlong porcelain vase stood out among thousands of mostly fake Chinese art submissions

Carved through ruby enamel to reveal white lotus patterns, the sgraffiato technique behind this vase

A rare large ruby-ground sgraffiato yangcai 'lotus' bottle vase, Seal mark and period of Qianlong (Image: Sotheby's)

No other vase of this design appears to survive: Seal mark of a rare Qianlong piece

The vase descended through Dame Agnes Jekyll 's family and sat in a Cornish house

What the £304,800 result shows about reviewing family heirlooms through online portals

A large imperial porcelain vase, standing thirty-seven centimetres tall and made for the Qianlong emperor, passed down through a single English family before arriving at Sotheby's. Estimated at between £100,000 and £200,000, it sold in November 2025 for £304,800, comfortably above the top end of the estimate. Its story combines rare craftsmanship, an ownership history leading back to a famous collecting family, and a surprising appearance in a property brochure. Here’s why a Sotheby's specialist called it pure gold, how the design was made, and what it can teach anyone with an old family treasure at home.Every day, Sotheby's receives unexpected objects through its online submissions portal, where owners upload a few photographs of something they suspect might be valuable. In Chinese art, that flood is overwhelming. Julian King, International Specialist in Chinese Works of Art at Sotheby's, said that the vast majority of the thousands of submissions the auction house receives in this category turn out to be fake, which makes a genuine piece exceptionally rare.This vase was different. King recognised it on sight, "This vase is pure gold," he said. The auction house catalogued it as lot sixty-one in its Chinese Art sale, listing it as property from an English family collection, according to the Sotheby's lot page.The Sotheby's lot page explains that sgraffiato, also spelt sgraffito, means carving through a surface layer to reveal a contrasting layer below. Here, the carving cuts through ruby enamel down to the glazed porcelain, revealing the design in white. Although the method came to prominence in China as early as the Song dynasty, it returned to the fore in the eighteenth century alongside the yangcai palette, whose name means foreign colours. The catalogue note, citing the research of Liao Pao Show, links its introduction at the imperial kilns in Jingdezhen to efforts from 1741 onwards by Tang Ying, the long-time kiln supervisor, to please the Qianlong emperor who had criticised earlier porcelain. In other words, this painstaking technique was refined partly to satisfy a demanding ruler.Few objects can claim to be unique, yet the Sotheby's catalogue note says no other vase of this extraordinary design appears to survive. The note describes the form as the classical yuhuchunping shape, popular since the Song dynasty, combined with brilliant ruby enamelling, baroque-inspired scrollwork and intricate sgraffiato. The vase stands thirty-seven centimetres tall, and its base carries a six-character seal mark in underglaze blue. Most related vases appear to have been made in pairs for the Qianlong court, and the note points to comparable examples in the Palace Museum in Beijing, the Yale University Art Gallery and the Hakone Museum of Art in Japan. That context helps explain why Sotheby's describes the piece as a rare and exuberant example of Qianlong taste.Authenticity was only part of the story. According to Sotheby's, the provenance, meaning the documented ownership history of an object, proved decisive. The lot page records the vase as belonging to the collection of Dame Agnes Lowndes Jekyll, who lived from 1861 to 1937, and passed to her by descent. Sotheby's describes her as a Scottish-born British artist, writer and philanthropist from a prominent collecting family; her father, William Graham, was a patron of Pre-Raphaelite artists. The vase was illustrated in an estate agent's brochure for the Cornish house where it had long sat. A piece of imperial porcelain had, in effect, been pictured to help sell a property, a reminder that remarkable objects can sit quietly in everyday domestic settings for many years.According to Sotheby's, the vase sold in 2025 for £304,800, well above its estimate of £100,000 to £200,000 for the auction held on 5 November. It is one of five recent success stories gathered by Sotheby's, all of which began with little more than a few photographs and a hunch. Many people never make the first move, assuming an auction house is meant for someone else's treasures rather than their own. Auction houses like Sotheby's describe their submission portal as one of the most accessible doors into the auction house, and it invites owners to share details and photos for a complimentary online estimate. If a family object has sat unexamined for years, this vase is a persuasive reason to ask a specialist to take a look.
Article Summary: The Qianlong porcelain vase sold for £304,800 at Sotheby's in 2025. It was made for the Qianlong emperor in the 17th century. The sgraffiato technique was developed to please the emperor. The vase was passed down through a single English family.

Article Title: He started farming on just 1 acre as a student; today his California family farm has 28 greenhouses and 500 customers: Meet Juan Perez
Article Text:
Juan Perez. Image Credit: California State University

A student turned 1 acre land into a California family farm

Three internships helped him discover his future

How the farm turned into a family-run operation with 28 greenhouses

Fresh produce connects the farm with its community

Perez believes a small farm can make a difference

Juan Perez did not set out to become a farmer when he enrolled at California State University, Monterey Bay. Yet a series of summer internships helped him discover a career that brought together his interest in science, his family’s farming experience and a desire to build something of his own. What began with a single leased acre has grown into J&P Organics, a family-run organic farm in California’s Salinas Valley. Today, the business grows fresh produce on 10 acres and supplies weekly farm boxes to more than 500 local customers.Perez’s journey into farming began with uncertainty about his future. His father, Pablo, had spent decades working on farms, and Juan had occasionally worked alongside him. However, his father encouraged him either to work with him or pursue higher education and find another career.As the first member of his family to attend university, Juan chose to study at California State University, Monterey Bay. He selected the university partly because it was only a 20-minute drive from his parents’ home in Castroville, allowing him to live on campus while returning home on weekends.Finding the right subject took time. He initially considered liberal studies, business administration and computer science, but none felt like a suitable fit.A science course eventually caught his attention, particularly the opportunity to conduct research outdoors and work on practical projects.According to Juan Perez’s alumni profile published by California State University, the turning point came when a professor encouraged him to apply for a summer internship at an organic farm. At first, the paid opportunity appealed mainly because he needed money for books, clothes and food. He had little idea that it would influence his career so profoundly. Perez launched J&P Organics with his father a year before walking at his university commencement in 2007. He later completed his capstone project in 2009 and earned a bachelor’s degree in environmental science, technology and policy. The idea was straightforward. Juan had gained knowledge of organic farming, while Pablo brought decades of experience in agriculture. Together, they could combine those strengths and create a family business.His father initially had reservations because he was unfamiliar with organic growing methods. Juan explained that the approach avoided pesticides and chemical treatments, and Pablo agreed to give it a try.Their first step was modest. With a $5,000 loan from the California Coastal Rural Development Corporation, the father and son leased 1 acre of land. They gradually added a second and third acre, eventually expanding to six acres before an opportunity arose to purchase a 10-acre farm in Salinas.According to California State University’s account of Perez’s journey, the same organisation helped them buy the property in 2013, turning their growing operation into a more permanent family enterprise.The first internship introduced Perez to the practical side of organic agriculture. He researched fertilisers, seeds and pest control, while also creating a small information library that other organic growers could use. The work suited him, and he began to see farming as more than a family connection.His professor, Bill Head, then encouraged him to complete a second summer internship at another organic farm. This experience broadened his understanding of the business, introducing him to marketing, farm-box sales and ways to encourage community support for agriculture.A third internship helped him build connections with people in the farming industry and gain confidence in his own abilities. By the end of that placement, Perez felt ready to start a business of his own.The Salinas property has developed into a working farm equipped with 28 commercial greenhouses, a packing shed, delivery vans, tractors, a private water well, fruit trees and open fields. These facilities support the daily work of growing, preparing and distributing produce.Despite its expansion, J&P Organics remains a close-knit family business. Juan and Pablo manage daily operations alongside Juan’s brother, Jose, who works as a mechanic. His mother, Florencia, helps with planting, transplanting, harvesting and packing, while his sister, Cristina, manages the taxes. Juan’s wife, Wendy, supports the business by handling calls, messages, customer questions and orders.The California State University profile notes that four families depend on the farm. Rather than employing an outside workforce, the family shares the responsibilities of running the operation.J&P Organics grows USDA-certified organic fruits, vegetables and flowers. Each week, customers receive an email explaining which produce will be included in their farm boxes. Orders are then delivered to homes or designated collection points.The farm serves more than 500 local customers, offering them a direct connection to the people who grow their food. Perez has explained in his California State University alumni profile that customers appreciate produce picked shortly before delivery. Even soil left on freshly harvested carrots can reassure buyers that their food has come straight from the ground. Customers can also visit the farm for pick-your-own days, allowing them to experience where their food comes from.The farm operates in the Salinas Valley, a region widely known for its agricultural production and favourable growing conditions. Its mild climate allows crops to be cultivated throughout the year, across winter, spring, summer and autumn.Perez believes that smaller organic farms can contribute to healthier food choices and more responsible care of the land. While the surrounding region includes much larger agricultural operations, he sees his own farm’s contribution in providing local families with fresh vegetables grown without conventional chemical pesticides.Education is another part of that commitment. As reported by California State University, Perez regularly welcomes elementary and secondary school pupils through the Monterey Bay Aquarium’s WATCH programme. He also hosts college student groups, giving them opportunities to learn about farming through direct experience.
Article Summary: Juan Perez started J&P Organics with his father, Pablo, in 2007. The farm has grown into a family-run operation with 28 greenhouses. The business supplies weekly farm boxes to more than 500 local customers. Perez believes a small farm can make a difference to the community.

Article Title: Strong 6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan
Article Text:
6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan

More details awaited

An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday, around 95 km south of Sūrāb, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC).The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles).
